questions.prompt: State the squeeze theorem in words.
questions.answer: If a function \(f(x)\) is trapped between two functions \(g(x)\) and \(h(x)\) near \(a\), and both outside functions approach the same limit \(L\), then \(f(x)\) also approaches \(L\).

questions.prompt: What are the three ingredients needed to use the squeeze theorem?
questions.answer:
You need an inequality
\[g(x)\le f(x)\le h(x)\]
near the approach point, the limit \(\lim g(x)\), and the limit \(\lim h(x)\).
The two outside limits must be equal.

questions.prompt: If \(-x^2\le f(x)\le x^2\) near \(0\), what is \(\lim_{x\to0}f(x)\)?
questions.answer:
Both bounding functions approach \(0\):
\[\lim_{x\to0}(-x^2)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to0}x^2=0.\]
Since \(f(x)\) is squeezed between them,
\[\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=0.\]

questions.prompt: Why is \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\) useful when evaluating limits near \(x=0\)?
questions.answer:
The function \(\sin(1/x)\) oscillates rapidly near \(0\), but it is always bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\).
Multiplying this bound by a factor that tends to \(0\), such as \(x^2\), can squeeze the whole product to \(0\).

Since \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\), multiply by \(x^2\ge0\):
\[-x^2\le x^2\sin(1/x)\le x^2.\]
Both bounds tend to \(0\).
By the squeeze theorem,
\[\lim_{x\to0}x^2\sin(1/x)=0.\]

Use \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\). Since \(|x|\ge0\), write
\[-|x|\le x\sin(1/x)\le |x|.\]
As \(x\to0\), both \(-|x|\) and \(|x|\) approach \(0\).
So the limit is \(0\).

Compute the outer limits:
\[\lim_{x\to0}(2-x^2)=2,\qquad \lim_{x\to0}(2+x^2)=2.\]
Since both bounds approach \(2\), the squeeze theorem gives
\[\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=2.\]

Because \(-1\le\cos(3/x)\le1\), and \(x^4\ge0\),
\[-x^4\le x^4\cos(3/x)\le x^4.\]
Both bounds approach \(0\) as \(x\to0\).
Therefore
\[\lim_{x\to0}x^4\cos(3/x)=0.\]

Use \(-1\le\cos(1/x^2)\le1\). Since \(x^2\ge0\),
\[-x^2\le x^2\cos(1/x^2)\le x^2.\]
Both outer functions tend to \(0\).
Thus the squeezed limit is
\[0.\]

Since \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\),
\[2\le3+\sin(1/x)\le4.\]
Multiply by \(x^2\ge0\):
\[2x^2\le x^2(3+\sin(1/x))\le4x^2.\]
Both bounds approach \(0\), so the limit is \(0\).

questions.prompt: Explain why the inequality in the squeeze theorem only needs to hold near the approach point, not necessarily at the point itself.
questions.answer:
A limit depends on values of the functions for \(x\) close to the approach point with \(x\ne a\).
The functions may be undefined or behave differently at \(a\).
Therefore the squeezing inequality must hold in a deleted neighborhood around \(a\), but it does not need to hold at \(a\) itself.

Since \(|\sin(5/x)|\le1\),
\[|x\sin(5/x)|=|x|\,|\sin(5/x)|\le |x|.\]
Also \(|x\sin(5/x)|\ge0\).
Thus
\[0\le |x\sin(5/x)|\le |x|.\]
Both bounds tend to \(0\), so the limit is \(0\).

questions.prompt: Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}x^2\left\lfloor\frac1{x^2}\right\rfloor\), where \(\lfloor y\rfloor\) is the greatest integer less than or equal to \(y\).
questions.answer:
For \(x\ne0\),
\[\left\lfloor\frac1{x^2}\right\rfloor\le\frac1{x^2}\]
and it is nonnegative. Multiplying by \(x^2>0\),
\[0\le x^2\left\lfloor\frac1{x^2}\right\rfloor\le1.\]
These bounds do not squeeze to a single value, so this inequality alone is insufficient. In fact the expression is close to \(1\), not \(0\), because
\[\frac1{x^2}-1<\left\lfloor\frac1{x^2}\right\rfloor\le\frac1{x^2}.\]
Multiplying gives
\[1-x^2<x^2\left\lfloor\frac1{x^2}\right\rfloor\le1,\]
so the limit is \(1\).

For \(x>0\),
\[\frac1x-1<\left\lfloor\frac1x\right\rfloor\le\frac1x.\]
Multiplying by \(x>0\),
\[1-x<x\left\lfloor\frac1x\right\rfloor\le1.\]
As \(x\to0^+\), both \(1-x\) and \(1\) approach \(1\).
By the squeeze theorem, the right-hand limit is \(1\).

Since \(0\le\sin^2(1/x)\le1\), multiply by \(x^2\ge0\):
\[0\le x^2\sin^2(1/x)\le x^2.\]
Both outer bounds approach \(0\), so the squeeze theorem gives
\[\lim_{x\to0}x^2\sin^2(1/x)=0.\]

For \(x\ne0\),
\[\frac{x^2}{|x|}=|x|.\]
So
\[\frac{x^2\sin(1/x)}{|x|}=|x|\sin(1/x).\]
Using \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\),
\[-|x|\le |x|\sin(1/x)\le |x|.\]
Both bounds tend to \(0\), so the limit is \(0\).

questions.prompt: A student tries to squeeze \(\sin(1/x)\) between \(-1\) and \(1\) and concludes \(\lim_{x\to0}\sin(1/x)=0\). Diagnose the error.
questions.answer:
The bounds \(-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1\) do not approach the same number.
The squeeze theorem requires both outer functions to have the same limit. Here the bounds are constant at \(-1\) and \(1\), so they do not squeeze to \(0\).
In fact \(\sin(1/x)\) oscillates and has no limit as \(x\to0\).

questions.prompt: Use the squeeze theorem with \(\cos x\le\frac{\sin x}{x}\le1\) near \(0\) to find \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}\).
questions.answer:
The inequality is
\[\cos x\le\frac{\sin x}{x}\le1\]
near \(0\) for \(x\ne0\).
The outer limits are
\[\lim_{x\to0}\cos x=1,\qquad \lim_{x\to0}1=1.\]
By the squeeze theorem,
\[\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1.\]

Use \(|\cos(1/x)|\le1\). Then
\[|x\cos(1/x)|=|x|\,|\cos(1/x)|\le |x|.\]
Also \(|x\cos(1/x)|\ge0\). Thus
\[0\le |x\cos(1/x)|\le |x|.\]
Since \(|x|\to0\), the absolute value tends to \(0\). Therefore
\[x\cos(1/x)\to0.\]

The inequality
\[|f(x)-3|\le(x-2)^2\]
means the distance from \(f(x)\) to \(3\) is bounded by \((x-2)^2\).
Since
\[\lim_{x\to2}(x-2)^2=0,\]
we have
\[0\le |f(x)-3|\le(x-2)^2.\]
By the squeeze theorem, \(|f(x)-3|\to0\), so \(f(x)\to3\).
